 6                    1.      Rate of Return on Capital and Cost of Capital Are Not the Same: Rate
 7                            of Return on Capital Is a Financial Performance Metric; Cost of
 8                            Capital Is a Measure of Economic Cost.

 9   Q. What should be the Commission’s goal in authorizing the rate of return?
10   A. The rate of return is the total return on capital that utilities are allowed to recover in customer
11         rates. The Commission’s duty in setting the authorized rate of return is to determine the
12         amount of each source of capital – common equity, preferred equity, and debt in this
13         proceeding – and a return on each that is as close as possible to the actual, market-based cost
14         of each source of capital.
15            The economic question is whether that return is no higher than necessary to compensate
16         investors for supplying capital to the utility’s rate base. When a return materially above the
17         cost of capital is applied to rate base, the result is excess earnings that customers are required
18         to fund without any corresponding benefit to reliability or utility capital access.
19
20   Q. How does the rate of return on capital differ from the cost of capital?
21   A. The rate of return on capital, often shortened to “rate of return,” is a measure of financial
22         performance, calculated by dividing the value returned to investors – e.g., interest, preferred
23         dividend, net income – by the amount of capital invested.
24            The cost of capital, by definition, is the return investors expect on their investment. It is
25         referred to as a cost because it reflects what investors demand in return for assuming the risk
26         of the investment and, therefore, what companies must pay for that investment.
27            The rate of return on each form of capital, whether calculated retrospectively or
28         estimated prospectively, may or may not equal its respective cost of capital.
29
30   Q. Why is the distinction between the cost of capital and rate of return important?
31   A. The cost of capital and rate of return (on capital) are entirely different concepts. The rate of
32         return is a financial performance metric. The cost of capital is a well-defined economic

 1      concept. Nonetheless, the terms “cost of capital” and “rate of return” are frequently referred
 2      to interchangeably in utility regulatory proceedings. This is not accepted practice among
 3      finance professionals and academics. A utility’s ROE may or may not be equal to the market-
 4      based COE, and the terms are not interchangeable.
 5         The muddling of the difference between the cost of capital and the rate of return is not
 6      just of semantic concern, particularly when calculating the return on equity. Unlike
 7      outstanding debt, whose cost of capital can be directly observed from contractual interest
 8      rates, the cost of equity cannot be directly observed and must be estimated using various
 9      models.
10         This confusion between the cost of capital and the return on capital has infiltrated some
11      of the models commonly used in utility cost of capital proceedings to estimate the cost of
12      equity, including the risk premium model (RPM) used by EPE Witness Nelson. Wide use of
13      these models and their apparent influence on regulatory decisions does not render them
14      economically justifiable to provide a suitable basis for estimating the cost of equity. Only
15      methodologies that estimate the cost of equity should be used to determine the authorized
16      ROE, in accordance with the ROR=COC standard.

 3   Q. What is the legal basis for the ROR=COC standard?
 4   A. The legal basis for the ROR=COC standard derives from the seminal Bluefield and Hope
 5        cases. Bluefield established that a utility is entitled to earn its cost of capital:

 6                     A public utility is entitled to such rates as will permit it to earn a return on the
 7                     value of the property which it employs for the convenience of the public equal
 8                     to that generally being made at the same time and in the same general part of
 9                     the country on investments in other business undertakings which are attended
10                     by corresponding risks and uncertainties; … The return should be reasonably
11                     sufficient to assure confidence in the financial soundness of the utility and
12                     should be adequate, under efficient and economical management, to maintain
13                     and support its credit and enable it to raise the money necessary for the proper
14                     discharge of its public duties.18

15        The “return … equal to that … on investments in other business undertakings which are
16        attended by corresponding risks and uncertainties” is the cost of capital: the minimum

 2   Q. Why does the gap between authorized ROE and the cost of equity violate cost-of-service
 3        ratemaking principles?
 4   A. A core principle of utility regulation is cost-of-service ratemaking (COSR). As the name
 5        suggests, utilities are supposed to recover only actual, prudently incurred costs. This includes
 6        their costs of capital, both equity and debt. Excess ROEs violate this foundational regulatory
 7        principle.
 8            Utility management is accountable to shareholders for the value of their investment. A
 9        fundamental principle of finance – discounted present value – tells us that an asset’s value
10        will equal the cost of the initial investment if and only if its expected return is equal to its risk
11        adjusted cost of capital. As the expected return increases above the cost of capital, the value
12        relative to the initial investment increases. This relationship between ROE and stock market
13        value is not linear, i.e., a 10% increase in ROE, from, say, 10% to 11%, does not result in an
14        increase in the stock price of 10%, but of 13% to 20%. 48 Utilities therefore have a powerful
15        incentive to maximize ROE.
16            Beyond their direct impact on rates (which includes the incremental taxes owed on the
17        surplus profit), excess ROEs incentivize utilities to unnecessarily expand rate base at
18        customer expense. And because of the non-linear relationship between stock market value
19        and ROE, the greater the difference between ROE and COE, the stronger the incentive to
20        inflate investment.
21            This perverse incentive structure is not just hypothetical. As explained above, with M/B
22        ratios of roughly 2.0, every dollar of equity invested creates roughly two dollars of
23        shareholder value – a powerful incentive to maximize investment.
24            The customer harm of excess ROEs is therefore several-fold: the immediate costs of the
25        excess ROE; the incremental taxes owed on that excess ROE; the additional costs of
26        unnecessary investment, including its cost of capital; the surplus profit from excess ROE on
27        that unnecessary investment; and the associated taxes on that surplus profit. Excess ROEs’
28        amplification of customer harms is precisely why COSR is such a foundational principle of
29        utility regulation.

 4   Q. What do you mean by a competitive auction to determine the return on equity?
 5   A. A competitive equity auction replaces administrative discretion over the return on equity with
 6      market competition. Rather than inferring the cost of equity from contested models, the
 7      utility offers a small, defined slice of its equity to qualified investors, who bid the return they
 8      require. The clearing bid establishes the cost of equity transparently and, subject to
 9      Commission certification, becomes the authorized ROE for the utility’s equity as a whole.
10      What is sold is a sample; what is discovered is the price. The mechanism does not require the
11      utility to recapitalize or to change its ownership: the auctioned interest is small, and its
12      purpose is to reveal the return investors actually require, not to replace the utility’s existing
13      sources of equity.

15   Q. Why would an auction do a better job of pricing the return investors require than the
16      process used today?
17   A. Because an auction observes the cost of equity rather than estimating it. Every method now
18      used in rate cases – CAPM, DCF, risk premium – is an attempt to infer, from models and
19      proxy groups, what return investors would require if they were asked. Section III shows how
20      much turns on that inference: EPE Witness Nelson’s own CAPM produces 11.66% or 6.21%
21      depending on a single input, the forecast market return. An auction simply asks. The
22      investors who would actually supply the capital each state the minimum return at which they
23      will commit funds, and the clearing bid is, by construction, the lowest return at which the
24      offering is fully subscribed. That is the definition of the cost of equity, and it is established
25      not by argument but by capital actually committed at that price.

27      in the outcome, and the Commission must weigh assertions it cannot test against the market.
28      In an auction, a bidder who overstates its required return is simply not filled; a bidder who
29      understates it loses money on its own capital. Neither can be helped by a more persuasive
30      expert. And because an auction can be repeated periodically, the result tracks capital market
31      conditions as they change, without a new round of litigation each time.

15              equity – must be lower than the authorized ROE.

12   Q.      What is the difference between book and market value?

13   A.      Book value reflects the historical net capital invested in the utility – essentially, what

14           investors have put in. In contrast, market value reflects what investors are willing to pay

15           today to own the company, based on expected future earnings and risk. Investors cannot

16           buy utilities at book value; they must pay market value. Only the market value, therefore,

17           incorporates current investor expectations, which is why market value is the appropriate

18           basis for estimating the cost of equity. A return metric that is based on a non-market

19           value, by definition, is not a market-based cost of capital.
